Proportional blame is wrong, yet so is a clean conscience. A virtuous builder feels the weight of what their system did, and that feeling is part of being good. Bernard Williams described a lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, kills a child. He is not to blame, yet we would think less of him if he felt nothing more than a bystander. That feeling, agent-regret, attaches to what you did, not to what you did wrong.

Blame tracks fault, and the careful builders were not at fault, so the motion is false. But virtue is not just avoiding fault. A good person responds to having caused harm with grief, a wish to repair it, and changed attention, and those responses are owed even here.

A Stoic will object that fortune is not up to the builders, so any weight they carry for it is a false judgement that something bad happened to them, and the wise builder would set it down. The Stoic is right that guilt here would be false, but wrong that every response to unintended harm is a mistake. Agent-regret is not a false belief about fault; it is an accurate recognition that this harm came through my hands. Outcomes matter, but the deeper question is what kind of people this practice turns us into.

A good person carries the weight of harm they caused even when blameless, so proportional blame is mistaken, while a builder who shrugs reveals a defect of character. Aristotle thought the right feeling at the right time towards the right people is part of virtue. The right feeling for a builder whose system killed someone is not guilt, which would be false, but neither is it the calm of someone who checked the boxes. The calm is the defect.

Character shows in how we carry what we did not intend. A team that says it followed procedure and moves on teaches its juniors that the procedure is the whole of responsibility. A team that sits with the harm teaches them that people, not procedures, are what they answer to. A surgeon who loses a patient despite perfect technique does not blame herself, but she does not go to lunch as if nothing happened.

A good answer has to come from good character, and good character cannot be replaced by a formula.

A good person responds to having caused harm with grief, a wish to repair it, and changed attention, and those responses are owed even here. Imagine an engineer who learns her model contributed to a death and says only that the audit was passed. Nothing she said is false, and something is still badly wrong.

A utilitarian will object that if the builders are not to blame then their feelings are their own business, and what matters is compensating victims and preventing future harm. Feelings are not private ornaments; they shape what people attend to. Builders who feel the weight of past harm look harder for the next one, and an institution that treats regret as irrelevant gradually stops noticing who it hurts. So the real question is what a person of practical wisdom would do here, and what doing otherwise would make of us.
